subject: Banking
title: Silicon Valley Bank: 48-Hour Collapse
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Silicon Valley Bank: 48-Hour Collapse.

hook.text: Silicon Valley Bank collapsed in 48 hours in March 2023.

buildup.text: SVB invested deposits in long-term government bonds. When the Fed raised rates, those bonds lost $15 billion in value.

discovery.text: 96% of SVB deposits were above the $250,000 FDIC insurance limit. Tech startups held millions per account.

twist.text: The FDIC stepped in and guaranteed ALL deposits, even uninsured ones.

climax.text: SVB was the first social media bank run. Twitter and group chats spread panic faster than any 1930s headline could.

punchline.text: $42 billion in one day. The first bank run driven by apps and tweets.

quiz.question: What percentage of SVB deposits were above the FDIC insurance limit?

details.summary: Silicon Valley Bank collapsed in just 48 hours in March 2023 after a failed stock offering triggered a social media-driven bank run. Depositors withdrew $42 billion in a single day, making it the fastest bank failure in modern history.
details.whyItMatters: SVB proved that digital bank runs can destroy an institution at speeds that regulators cannot match. The failure exposed how rising interest rates create hidden losses in bank bond portfolios.
takeaways: SVB lost $42 billion in deposits in a single day
Its bond portfolio had $17 billion in unrealized losses from rising rates
93 percent of deposits exceeded the $250,000 FDIC insurance limit

faq.question: Why did Silicon Valley Bank fail so quickly?
faq.answer: SVB had invested heavily in long-term bonds that lost value as rates rose. When it tried to raise capital by selling bonds at a loss, social media-driven panic caused $42 billion in withdrawals in one day, far exceeding the bank's available cash.

faq.question: Were SVB depositors above the FDIC limit protected?
faq.answer: Yes. The FDIC, Treasury, and Fed jointly invoked a systemic risk exception to guarantee all deposits, including those above $250,000. This prevented potential contagion to other banks with similarly concentrated, largely uninsured deposit bases.
